problems.problem: This is not the best line of the day. Numbers 5 to 6 contains the Priestly Blessing (6:24 to 26), and day.js prints 6:26 as a whole, citable sentence (‘The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace.’, 11 words). The entry picks instead the Nazirite’s ban on corpse uncleanness, and its reading (an etymology Ibn Ezra only reports from others, plus a remark on freedom from desire) depends on ‘consecration’ standing for nezer, crown, a link the English key verse never shows the reader.
problems.fix: Use key Numbers 6:26 (confirm with verse.js). The packet for --verse 6:26 has Rashi, ‘יכבוש כעסו’ (may He suppress His anger), Rashbam (He will not hide His face, but turn to His beloved to be gracious), and Sforno on ‘וישם לך שלום’ (a rest of peace, lasting and free of punishment). For example: Closing the blessing Aaron and his sons are to speak over Israel; Rashi, on 6:26, reads the lifted countenance as God suppressing His anger, and Rashbam, on 6:26, as God not hiding His face but turning to His beloved to be gracious. Run the entry through entry-check.

problems.problem: The Ibn Ezra half does not parse cleanly. In ‘as the soul named because this is a freewill gift’, ‘the soul named’ reads as a noun with a participle, not as ‘the text names the soul’, and ‘this’ has no clear antecedent (the meal-offering). A reader has to stop to rebuild what Ibn Ezra says: nefesh is named because the meal-offering is a freewill gift and the soul too is called willing.
problems.fix: …, and Ibn Ezra, on 2:1, as naming the soul because the meal-offering is a freewill gift and the soul too is called willing. (The evidence is the same: Ibn Ezra on 2:1, ‘והזכיר הנפש שהמנחה נדבה גם הנפש תקרא נדיבה’. The sentence stays within 60 words.)
